title: The Voyaging of Hōkūleʻa
intro: Hōkūleʻa is a Polynesian double-hulled voyaging canoe (waʻa kaulua) launched on 8 March 1975 by the Polynesian Voyaging Society. Its 1976 voyage from Hawaiʻi to Tahiti was made with exclusively traditional navigation, under the Satawalese master navigator Pius "Mau" Piailug, and later voyages carried the canoe across Polynesia and, from 2014, around the world.
ending: Hōkūleʻa and its sister vessel Hikianalia returned to Hawaiʻi on 17 June 2017 after a three-year circumnavigation of 47,000 nautical miles, with stops at 85 ports in 26 countries.

stops.text: Hōkūleʻa left Honolua Bay on Maui for Tahiti, with Mau Piailug as navigator and Kawika Kapahulehua as captain, as part of the celebration of the United States Bicentennial.
stops.quote: Hōkūleʻa departed Honolua Bay, Maui, Hawaiʻi for Papeʻete, Tahiti,

stops.text: Mau Piailug navigated from Hawaiʻi to Tahiti without instruments. After a conflict among the crew escalated into physical violence, he returned home to Micronesia, and the canoe was navigated back with western instruments.
stops.quote: Mau navigated from Hawaii to Tahiti without instruments.

stops.text: Hōkūleʻa left Honolulu's Ala Wai Harbor on a second voyage to Tahiti, with Nainoa Thompson as navigator and Dave Lyman as captain.
stops.quote: attempted a second voyage to Tahiti, which was aborted when Hōkūleʻa capsized in high wind and seas southwest of the Island of Molokaʻi, five hours after departing Honolulu's Ala Wai Harbor.

stops.text: The canoe capsized southwest of Molokaʻi and the crew held on through the night. Eddie Aikau paddled a surfboard towards Lānaʻi for help and was never seen again. The crew were rescued by the Coast Guard and the canoe was towed back to Honolulu.
stops.quote: The following morning, the USCGC Cape Corwin towed the vessel, from 22 miles southwest of Lāʻau Point, Molokaʻi, back to Honolulu.

stops.text: After the 1978 disaster Mau Piailug returned and trained Nainoa Thompson further. Thompson set out from Hilo to recreate the 1976 voyage, with Mau sailing as an observer.
stops.quote: Hilo, Hawaiʻi Island,  United States – Papeʻete, Tahiti, Society Islands,  French Polynesia: 15 March 1980 to 17 April 1980

stops.text: After 29 days at sea, before sighting Mataiva, Mau offered Nainoa one correction: a seabird in mid-morning flight carrying a fish was flying towards land to feed its young, not away from it.
stops.quote: After 29 days at sea, before sighting Mataiva on the way to Tahiti, Mau offered Nainoa only one correction

stops.text: Thompson became the first Native Hawaiian in modern times to navigate a canoe thousands of miles without instruments, arriving in Tahiti after 29 days at sea.
stops.quote: In 1980, Nainoa Thompson recreated the 1976 voyage to Tahiti to become the first Native Hawaiian in modern times to navigate a canoe thousands of miles without instruments.

stops.text: Hōkūleʻa sailed from Papeʻete to Rarotonga in the Cook Islands, with Nainoa Thompson as navigator, on the first legs of a voyage of 12,000 miles to destinations throughout Polynesia.
stops.quote: Papeʻete, Tahiti,  French Polynesia – Rarotonga,  Cook Islands (map): 30 August 1985 to 14 September 1985

stops.text: The canoe sailed from Rarotonga to Waitangi on the North Island of New Zealand, with Nainoa Thompson as navigator and Shorty Bertelmann as captain.
Hōkūleʻa sailed from Waitangi to Nukuʻalofa on Tongatapu, with Leon Paoa Sterling as captain and Sione Uaine Ula of Tonga among the crew.
The canoe went on to Pago Pago on Tutuila in American Samoa. Hector Busby of New Zealand and Sione Taupeamuhu of Tonga were among the crew.
Hōkūleʻa sailed from Ofu Island in American Samoa to Aitutaki in the Cook Islands, with Shorty Bertelmann as captain and Tua Pittman of the Cook Islands among the crew.
After a short leg from Aitutaki back to Rarotonga, Hōkūleʻa sailed on to Tautira on Tahiti Iti. Nainoa Thompson was both navigator and captain.
In 1987 the canoe sailed from Tautira to Rangiroa Atoll in the Tuamotus, as the first step of the voyage home to Hawaiʻi.
Hōkūleʻa sailed from Rangiroa to Kualoa on Oʻahu, ending the Voyage of Rediscovery, with Shorty Bertelmann as captain and Nainoa Thompson as navigator.

legs.title: Malama Honua, the worldwide voyage, 2014 to 2017

stops.text: Hōkūleʻa and its sister vessel Hikianalia set out from Oʻahu on "Malama Honua", a three-year circumnavigation of the earth.
stops.quote: On 18 May 2014 Hōkūle‘a and its sister vessel, Hikianalia, embarked from Oahu for "Malama Honua," a three-year circumnavigation of the earth.

stops.text: In the Australian and Indian Ocean part of the voyage, Hōkūleʻa called at Bali in August 2015.
In the Atlantic part of the voyage, Hōkūleʻa stopped at Saint Helena in January 2016, on its way to Brazil.
stops.quote: January 2016 St. Helena, en route to Brazil

stops.text: Hōkūleʻa called at Havana, Cuba, in March 2016, after the US Virgin Islands in the Caribbean.
On the North American leg, Hōkūleʻa reached New York City in June 2016, after visiting Washington, D.C., in May.
Back in the Pacific after a two-day transit of the Panama Canal and a stop in the Galapagos in February, Hōkūleʻa reached Rapa Nui in March 2017.
Hōkūleʻa came home to Hawaiʻi, after calling at Tahiti in April. The homecoming took place at Magic Island, Oʻahu, on 17 June 2017.

notes: Source is Hōkūleʻa's Wikipedia article. Doubts for the editor: (1) Mataiva has no date in the article, so date and year are null; the stop sits between Hilo and Papeʻete as the article places it. (2) Magic Island has no article of its own that I can confirm; wp is 'Ala Moana Regional Park', which holds it, check the point. (3) Ala Wai Harbor wp 'Ala Wai Boat Harbor' and Hilo wp 'Hilo, Hawaii' are my best guesses at titles. (4) Honolua Bay, 1976: the article gives 1 May and 4 June 1976 on the line under the narrative, and the Papeʻete quote is the narrative sentence beside it. (5) The 1976 return to Hawaiʻi (5 to 26 July 1976) and the 1985 Hawaiʻi to Papeʻete leg name no mapped place, so both are left out. (6) The Tongatapu to Nomuka night passage is told without a date or position in the sequence; left out. (7) 1978: the capsizing date is the departure day, 16 March, in the article's 16 to 18 March range; Lāʻau Point has only 'March 1978'. (8) The 2014 to 2017 stops come from the article's month list, which gives months only; Hikianalia sailed as its sister vessel. Left out: the 1977 Kealaikahiki project, the 1992, 1995, 1999 to 2000, 2003 to 2004 and 2007 voyages, and Moananuiākea (2023 onward), to keep to 22 stops, though the article gives stops for them. The Rediscovery quotes are the leg dates beside each place's heading; the checker may not find them because of the flag symbols and double spaces.
